title: Names of weapons
hookLine: a long poem of weapon-names used as names of the Divine

cards: Axe. Musket. Say them in a row and they sound like an inventory, or a threat.

Now say them in a row as names for God. That's what one poem among Guru Gobind Singh's writings does. It's called Shastar Nam Mala, the garland of weapon names, and it reads like a rosary strung with blades.
For some listeners that's jarring, even unsettling. For Sikhs it is a way of seeing, and today is about what that way sees.

teach.b: Shastar means weapon, nam means name, and a mala is a garland, the same word used for a string of prayer beads.

The poem opens, paraphrased, by listing weapons, sword, kirpan, khanda, musket, axe and arrow, and calling them our pir, our guides. Then it moves through name after name of weapons, and through them names the Divine.
Why pray like that? Sikhs answer in a few connected ways.
First, a weapon here stands for power, and in Sikh teaching all power belongs to God. To name the blade is to name the One whose strength it borrows. Second, the power is for protection.
Sikhs speak of the sword as the defender of the weak, the thing that stands between the bully and the person being bullied.
The Zafarnama says it plainly, in paraphrase: when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first. Third, the poem trains attention.
A tool takes on the purpose of the hand that holds it. The same edge that cuts bread can wound. Naming it as God's is a reminder of whose purpose it must serve.
Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan, one of the five Ks from day eighteen, as an article of faith, not as an ornament and not as a threat. It's a vow worn at the hip.
Looking back over this week: still standing, protected, ten hymns, by their grace, the power remembered, true devotion. Today closes it with power held in the right hands.

how: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan as one of the articles of faith, and Sikh teachers explain it, and the weapon names of Shastar Nam Mala, as signs of God's power used to protect the weak.

games.why: in Shastar Nam Mala the weapon names become names of the Divine. for Sikhs, all power is God's, and it is for protection.

practice: Think through your day, your phone, your keys, your voice, your hands, a kitchen knife, a pen, and pick one.
Notice what it can do when it serves someone, and what it could do if it didn't, then give it a quiet job: this is for good. If you pray, offer it to Waheguru.
